vignette: Dong was a 40-year-old South Eastern Asian male who had been working as a journalist for over two decades. His career had often placed him in high-risk environments, but nothing could have prepared him for the trauma he experienced during an assignment abroad where he was tortured by a militant group. The harrowing event left deep psychological scars that manifested in various ways, making his daily life increasingly challenging. Since returning home, Dong found himself frequently triggered by ordinary sounds like children crying, which sent him into a state of intense distress. He had come to believe that these triggers were constant reminders of the violence he endured, and they often led him to feel dizzy or lightheaded. The sound of children crying was particularly potent because it reminded him of his own powerlessness during the torture when he heard similar cries from fellow captives. The memory of his ordeal was both fragmented and surreal. When Dong tried to deliberately recall what had happened, he found it difficult to access specific details, leaving parts of the event shrouded in mystery. He often felt that the memory was so extreme it was hard to believe it actually occurred. This made him feel as though others could see the trauma etched on his face, and he became convinced that there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. The violation of his values during the torture further compounded his sense of defectiveness. These negative appraisals significantly influenced Dong’s behavior and coping strategies. He avoided social contacts, finding it difficult to be around people he had once socialized with before the event. His fear that others could see what happened to him made these interactions particularly distressing. As a result, he began undereating as a way of coping, believing that controlling his physical state might give him some semblance of control over his emotions. The constant rumination on how the event could have been prevented only deepened his feelings of guilt and shame. This rumination often triggered a cycle where Dong would become hyper-vigilant, watching others closely for signs that they might harm him. He found himself startled by ordinary sounds, believing that these sounds were potential indicators of impending danger. Dong’s memory problems also contributed to his maladaptive strategies. The difficulty in recalling specific details made it hard for him to process the trauma fully, leading to a reliance on avoidance behaviors like undereating and social isolation. His tendency to ruminate on how the event could have been prevented further reinforced these coping mechanisms, as he believed that avoiding certain triggers would somehow prevent similar situations from occurring again. The intertwining of his negative appraisals with his maladaptive strategies created a self-reinforcing cycle. Dong’s belief in being defective and exposed often led him to avoid social interactions, which in turn exacerbated his fear that others could see what happened to him. This avoidance only reinforced his sense of isolation and made it harder for him to process the trauma. His work as a journalist had once been a source of pride, but now even mundane aspects of his job triggered intense emotional responses. The sound of a child crying on an interview recording or a dizzy spell while walking through a crowded newsroom became triggers that he found increasingly difficult to manage. His colleagues noticed changes in his behavior and often expressed concern, which only added to his sense of shame. What finally brought Dong to seek help was the realization that his daily life had become unbearable. He was most afraid of losing control completely and becoming unable to function at all. Yet, he also harbored a glimmer of hope that with professional support, he might find ways to cope more effectively and begin healing from the trauma. Dong’s story is one of persistent struggle and resilience, where the weight of his traumatic experience has shaped every aspect of his life. The intricate web of triggers, negative appraisals, memory difficulties, and maladaptive strategies creates a cycle that feels relentless. Yet, in recognizing the need for help, there lies a potential pathway towards recovery and reclaiming control over his life.
